  1. Polyrhythm
  2. What Is a Polyrhythm?

What Is a Polyrhythm?

Two rhythms at once: 3 against 2, 4 against 3 and 5 against 4, the grid that holds them, how to clap them, and how a polyrhythm differs from polymeter and hemiola.

A polyrhythm is two or more rhythms played at the same time that divide the same span of time into different numbers of even parts. In 3 against 2, one part plays three even notes while another plays two, and both start together. Each player on this page draws the cycle as a circle (the hand goes round once per cycle) and as a grid (time runs left to right). Click a layer’s name to mute it.

3 against 2

The two layers meet only on the first beat. In between, the notes fall at different places: the “two” lands exactly between the second and third “three”. A common way to say it is “nice cup of tea”:

Count six even pulses. The three falls on pulses 1, 3 and 5; the two on 1 and 4. Together they sound on pulses 1, 3, 4 and 5, one syllable each: nice (both), cup (three), of (two), tea (three).

Try it. Tap the three with your right hand on your knee and the two with your left. Mute one layer and play it yourself; then mute the other.

The grid underneath: least common multiple

To write two even layers on one grid, you need a pulse that both fit into. That pulse count is the least common multiple of the two numbers.

Polyrhythm Grid Layer A hits on pulse Layer B hits on pulse
3 : 2 6 1, 3, 5 1, 4
4 : 3 12 1, 4, 7, 10 1, 5, 9
5 : 4 20 every 4th every 5th
5 : 3 15 every 3rd every 5th

Below the player, the line under the grid shows the pulse count for whatever is playing.

4 against 3

A common saying for 4 against 3 is “pass the golden butter”, said evenly over twelve pulses. Hear the three as the beat first (it is the lower sound), then switch: mute the three, feel the four as the beat, and the three becomes the cross-rhythm.

5 against 4 and beyond

With bigger numbers no one counts the grid. Players hear the outer layer as a steady line that slides against the beat and meets it again at the start of the cycle.

Polyrhythm, polymeter and hemiola

These three words are often mixed up:

  • Polyrhythm: different even divisions of the same span (3 notes and 2 notes in one bar).
  • Polymeter: patterns of different lengths on the same pulse (a 5-step riff over 4-step bars). They drift apart and meet again after a while. The math rock lesson is about this.
  • Hemiola: three groups of two heard against two groups of three, as in 6/8 heard as 3/4. It is 3 against 2 at the level of beats.

This one is polymeter: every step is the same length. Watch the 5-step pattern start in a different place each bar until it lines up after 20 steps.

Make your own

The Polyrhythm tool lets you type layers, choose sounds and switch between polyrhythm and polymeter.
